subject: TrueCap #15 — cost segregation: the tax move most investors miss
preheader: Front-load 25-35% of depreciation · When the $4-7k study pays for itself · Honest limits

marketSnapshot.headline: Fed cut 50bp, mortgage rates broke 6.2%
marketSnapshot.body: Fed cut 50bp on Wednesday — the larger of the two scenarios. Mortgage rates dropped immediately, 30Y now at 6.18%. DSCR loans at 7.65%. This is the lowest rate environment in 14 months and the strongest setup for new acquisitions since early 2024. Three things investors are doing this week: (1) accelerating closings on deals that were in pending — locking the new lower rate. (2) running re-underwrites on saved deals from earlier in the year to see which ones now pencil at the lower rate. (3) considering refinancing existing 7-8% loans. Break-even on refi at this rate level is typically 18-28 months depending on closing costs.

dealSpotter.body: $315k 3/2 at $2,100 rent. I underwrote this in June at 6.85% and called it Marginal — cash flow was $80/mo, DSCR 1.18. At today's 6.18%, cash flow is $245/mo, DSCR 1.31. Same property, same rents, same underwriting — just the rate change took it from 'skip' to 'go.' This is happening across dozens of deals — worth re-running anything you walked from earlier in the year.

Including this not as a new deal but as a refi callout. If you closed this property in 2024 at 7.5%, today's 6.18% is a 132bp drop. On a $400k loan, that's ~$385/mo of savings. Closing costs typically $5-7k. Break-even = 13-18 months. If you plan to hold past then, refinance. Get 3 quotes — rate variance between lenders is wider than usual right now.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 8.4% cap at new rates · clean play
dealSpotter.body: $215k 3/2 at $1,950 rent. Already a strong deal at 6.85%. At 6.18%, cash flow improves another $115/mo, taking total monthly NCF to $850. Cap rate unchanged at 8.4% (cap rate is rate-agnostic), but the financed return is meaningfully better.

blogFeature.title: 1031 exchange basics: how to defer capital gains on rental property
blogFeature.excerpt: 1031 + cost segregation pair well — defer the gain on the sold property, accelerate depreciation on the replacement. The two-step tax strategy that materially improves IRR for tax-aware investors.

qa.question: Cost segregation: my CPA says it's worth doing on my $400k rental. How does it actually work?
qa.answer: Cost seg breaks your building into components — land improvements, personal property, systems — that depreciate over 5, 7, or 15 years instead of the standard 27.5 years for residential rental property. On a typical SFR, 20-30% of the building value gets reclassified to faster depreciation schedules. The result: in years 1-5 of ownership, your depreciation deduction is 2-3x what it would be without the study. The math on your $400k rental: assume $80k is reclassified to 5-15 year schedules. You front-load ~$50-65k of depreciation deductions into the first 5 years vs spreading it across 27.5. At a 32% effective tax bracket, that's $16-21k of accelerated tax savings in those first 5 years. Cost of the engineering study: typically $4-7k. So you'd save ~$12-16k net over the first 5 years, plus a meaningful time-value-of-money benefit on the front-loaded deductions. The catch: when you sell, the front-loaded depreciation gets 'recaptured' at ordinary income rates (vs the 25% rate on standard depreciation recapture). So cost seg is best for properties you'll hold 7+ years or 1031-exchange. If you're flipping or selling in 2-3 years, the math doesn't usually work.
